video_title: Stephanie Pomboy: Rising Bond Yields Are EVERYONE'S Problem
gist: Stephanie Pomboy argues the AI capex boom is itself the cause of higher-for-longer rates: hyperscalers have gone free-cash-flow negative and are now issuing debt into a market that already has to absorb a $10 trillion federal roll, so corporate borrowers are crowding out the government and pushing the long end of the Treasury curve higher. She also contends reported S&P earnings are inflated roughly 2x by mark-to-market gains on private AI stakes (Amazon's Anthropic position went from $8B to north of $75B), that buybacks have flipped to net equity issuance, and that a ~$4 trillion pension funding hole plus alternative-asset marks at 50 cents on the dollar makes an eventual pension bailout and a $15-20 trillion Fed balance sheet the likely endgame — which is why she stays long hard assets, energy and gold.

insights.claim: Amazon's stake in Anthropic has gone from an initial ~$8 billion investment to a valuation north of $75 billion, and those unrealized mark-to-market gains flow through the income statement as 'other income' rather than operating cash.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Any markdown in private AI valuations reverses directly into reported EPS for Amazon and peers, so headline earnings multiples on hyperscalers are levered to a private-market mark investors cannot observe.
insights.quote: their initial investment into Anthropic was 8 billion and the latest valuation I saw of Amazon's uh position there was now something north of 75 billion

insights.claim: In a recent quarter Amazon reported roughly $30 billion of earnings, of which about $16 billion was appreciation in its Anthropic stake — meaning roughly half the purported earnings growth was a bookkeeping item unrelated to paying salaries, funding capex or servicing debt.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Strip the mark and the cash-generative core of the largest index weight looks far weaker than the print, which matters for anyone underwriting index EPS.
insights.quote: their reported earnings were something like let's say 30 billion of which 16 billion was the appreciation in their anthropic stake

insights.claim: A study of first-quarter S&P 500 earnings showed roughly 20% year-on-year growth, of which about 12 percentage points was mark-to-market accounting — implying real earnings growth was roughly half the headline.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Index-level earnings momentum used to justify record highs is materially overstated; a stall in private AI marks alone could halve reported growth.
insights.quote: first quarter S&P earnings were something around 20% growth yearon-year and his analysis showed that you know 12% of that was just this marktomarket accounting

insights.claim: The dozen or so mega-cap companies whose cash hoards made the S&P 500 look cash-rich are now all free cash flow negative, meaning the aggregate corporate balance-sheet strength narrative was concentrated in names that have since flipped.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: The 'corporate America is flush with cash' argument for equity resilience is now empirically dead; watch aggregate S&P cash ex-mega-cap.
insights.quote: It turned out it was actually only like 12 companies all of whom are now free cash flow negative.

insights.claim: Google booked a large chunk of a recent quarter's earnings from gains on its Anthropic stake, making that portion of its profit one-time rather than recurring.
insights.speaker: host (Adam)
insights.so_what: If Anthropic is overvalued, Google's reported earnings are overvalued by construction — a direct link between private AI marks and public mega-cap P/Es.
insights.quote: in the case of Google a big chunk of its um latest earnings came from booking gains and its stake in anthropic

insights.claim: A large depreciation wave from AI data-center investment has not yet hit hyperscaler income statements; adjusting for depreciation and one-time gains takes the effective P/E on some of these companies from the teens or low 20s to roughly 65.
insights.speaker: host (Adam), citing Fred Hickey
insights.so_what: The depreciation schedule is the single biggest lever on forward AI-infrastructure earnings; watch useful-life assumptions in 10-Ks for the first crack.
insights.quote: if you adjust it the way that that he adjusts it, he's like it's more like 65

insights.claim: If the AI bubble bursts, hyperscalers face a double hit — operational earnings damage plus mandatory booking of massive losses on their marked-up private AI stakes.
insights.speaker: host (Adam)
insights.so_what: Downside earnings scenarios for mega-caps are non-linear because the mark-to-market gearing works in reverse.

themes.theme: Hyperscaler Credit Stress and Widening Spreads

insights.claim: Hyperscalers are issuing debt aggressively and their borrowing spreads are widening on concerns about overinvestment, pushing their interest costs up even as equity markets ignore the signal.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Credit is pricing AI overbuild risk before equities do — hyperscaler spreads and CDS are the leading indicator to monitor for the equity turn.
insights.quote: the spreads on this hyperscaler uh borrowing are starting to widen out around you know concerns about overinvestment etc. So you are seeing interest costs go up.

insights.claim: The credit default swap market is showing increased cost of insuring against hyperscaler default, a discernment that has not yet transmitted into broad equity-market concern.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: A tradable divergence: long hyperscaler CDS / short equity risk premium, or simply use CDS as the timing signal for equity de-risking.
insights.quote: what you're seeing in the credit markets is a real uh increasing discernment around uh the hyperscalers in terms of widening spreads, increased you know cost of insuring against default, the credit default swap market

insights.claim: The binding constraint on the AI capex buildout may shift from physical inputs to capital availability, because hyperscalers are increasingly dependent on credit and dearer credit mechanically shrinks how much they can afford to borrow.
insights.speaker: host (Adam)
insights.so_what: Capex schedules in sell-side models assume capital is unlimited; rising funding costs are the most quantifiable way those schedules get cut.
insights.quote: These companies are becoming increasingly dependent on credit to do this buildout and the credit is becoming more expensive and the more expensive credit becomes, the less credit these companies can afford to take out.

themes.theme: Crowding Out: $10T Treasury Roll and the Vanished Buyback Bid

insights.claim: The US Treasury must roll roughly $10 trillion of debt this year — about $6.7 trillion of T-bills that automatically roll every 12 months plus roughly $2.3-3.3 trillion of bonds and notes.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: This is the supply backdrop every duration trade must clear; auction tails and term-premium expansion are the transmission channel.
insights.quote: we have 6.7 trillion in T bills that automatically have to be rolled every 12 months, plus we have an additional 2.3 trillion or or 3.3 trillion in bonds and notes uh this year

insights.claim: Corporate borrowers are now crowding out the federal government — a reversal of the textbook direction — because the private sector's funding needs are competing directly for the same pool of capital.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Reframes the yield story: term premium is being driven by private issuance, not just deficits, so fiscal restraint alone would not fix the long end.
insights.quote: right now the corporate borrowers are ironically crowding out the federal government

insights.claim: SIFMA bond-issuance data show the private sector has borrowed the same amount as the federal government so far this year, an unprecedented level of private paper supply.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: A hard, checkable dataset for tracking the crowding-out thesis quarter by quarter.
insights.quote: the private sector has borrowed thus far this year the same amount as the federal government which is just mindboggling

insights.claim: The corporate sector entered this year needing to roll roughly $1.2 trillion of its own existing paper, on top of federal, municipal and agency needs, before hyperscaler incremental borrowing was even added.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Quantifies the queue of issuance competing for a finite bid; supports a structurally higher clearing yield.
insights.quote: the corporate sector needed to roll 1.2 two trillion of its own existing paper

insights.claim: With abundant high-quality corporate paper on offer, investors no longer have to buy Treasuries at all — a Google-quality credit at a higher yield is a substitute, and the long end of the Treasury curve is paying the price with a large backup in the 30-year and 10-year.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Explains long-end weakness as a relative-value substitution problem, implying steepeners persist until corporate supply slows.
insights.quote: if I thought, you know, Google was a a better quality credit than the federal government, lend money to them because there's now that opportunity

insights.claim: The Bank of Japan's defense of the yen requires selling dollars, most easily done by selling Treasury holdings, adding further upward pressure on US yields.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Yen weakness is a direct, monitorable input to US long-end yields — watch BoJ intervention headlines as a Treasury supply event.
insights.quote: the Bank of Japan intervening hasn't helped because they're trying to support the yen. And the way you support the yen is by selling dollars, which is most easily done by selling some of their Treasury holdings

insights.claim: Being bullish on AI capex mechanically implies being bullish on higher-for-longer rates, because the capex boom is what feeds the crowding-out that lifts the Treasury benchmark everyone else is priced off.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: The central non-obvious link of the episode: AI bulls are implicitly short duration, and long-duration equity valuations cannot both win.
insights.quote: the higher for longer interest rate environment I think is very much here to stay especially if you're bullish on AI and this whole capex boom because that's going to feed this crowding out phenomenon

insights.claim: Even if corporate spreads compress further from levels described as about as tight as they can get, nominal borrowing yields for these companies will still be the highest in many years.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Spread tightening is not a rescue — the all-in cost of capital is set by the risk-free base, so refinancing math deteriorates regardless.
insights.quote: Even if spreads compress a little bit farther from here, which is, you know, they're already about as tight as they can get. But even if they compress farther, you're still talking about nominal yields that are going to be the highest in in many years

insights.claim: Companies have stopped buying back shares and are now net issuers of stock, removing a source of demand that had run over a trillion dollars a year and at times made the corporate sector the largest single buyer of equities.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: A quiet, quantifiable withdrawal of the biggest structural equity bid — track net issuance data as a flow headwind independent of earnings.
insights.quote: companies have stopped buying back shares. They are now net issuers of stock. This is another huge uh negative for the stock market

insights.claim: Retail investors have become the more aggressive marginal buyer of equities as corporate buybacks faded, shifting who is absorbing supply.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: A retail-dominated bid is more fragile than a price-insensitive corporate bid, raising drawdown severity in a risk-off.
insights.quote: you've gotten to the point where retail investors have really become more aggressive

insights.claim: Simultaneous record credit issuance and rising equity issuance raise the question of whether the supply of capital is finite, since demands for capital across government, corporates, municipalities and hyperscalers are unprecedented.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Treat total paper supply — debt plus equity — as the scarce-capital variable driving both yields and equity multiples.
insights.quote: we have this environment where we've got massive credit issuance. We've never seen numbers like this before

insights.claim: The Fed funds rate is largely irrelevant to the problem because the last several times the Fed moved it, the long end of the yield curve moved in the opposite direction — only the balance sheet gives the Fed real leverage over long rates.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Positioning off FOMC cut expectations misses the driver; balance-sheet policy announcements are the tradable event for duration.
insights.quote: forget about the Fed funds rate. All this fixation on the Fed funds rates irrelevant because we've seen already the last several times they've moved it. the long end of the yield curve has gone in the opposite direction

insights.claim: Kevin Warsh's platform of shrinking the Fed balance sheet and possibly raising rates is the exact opposite of what the crowding-out problem requires, and it ignores who becomes the buyer of last resort for Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Sets up a policy-credibility break: expect the hawkish program to be abandoned, which is a duration and gold catalyst.
insights.quote: this is why I' I've always struggled with Kevin Worsh's plan because it seemed to ignore what was the elephant in the room, which is who's going to who's going to be the buyer of last resort for treasuries

insights.claim: Despite stated resistance to balance-sheet expansion, the Fed's balance sheet is already up over $200 billion since it started what Pomboy calls 'non-QE QE' back in December.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Actual reserve growth contradicts hawkish rhetoric — a concrete weekly H.4.1 series to track versus official guidance.
insights.quote: It's up over 200 billion since they started nonQEQ back in December.

insights.claim: Scott Bessent campaigned on reducing reliance on T-bill issuance but found on taking office there was no way around it, so heavy bill issuance continues at least until long-term rates come down.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Front-loaded bill supply keeps the front end anchored to policy while leaving the long end exposed — supports curve steepening.
insights.quote: Besson came he campaigned on the idea that we can't rely on T billill issuance and then he got, you know, sat down at his desk the first day and sharpened his pencil and realized there was no way to get around relying on T bill issuance

insights.claim: A moderate credit crisis — large enough to shrink risk appetite and drive money out of corporate debt into Treasuries but not a 2008-scale event — would be the ideal relief valve for the long end, but it would come with corporate spreads blowing out.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Frames the only realistic path to lower yields as a credit accident — implying long-duration Treasuries are a hedge on corporate spread widening, not a growth trade.
insights.quote: the ideal scenario would actually be if we had a credit crisis I that wasn't, you know, a super large crisis like we had in 20089, but enough to get some risk appetite diminished and get people to start running into treasuries instead of into corporate debt

insights.claim: The administration is committed to what Darius Dale calls the 'run it hot' scenario — growing out of the debt problem — but faster growth and more capex simply pull the reckoning forward through overheating.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive: strong growth data is bearish for duration and accelerates the bust, so good macro prints are not risk-on for the long end.
insights.quote: the faster the economy grows, which is great, you know, and the more capex we pursue, um, the sooner we pull that reckoning forward just because you reach that overheating

insights.claim: The growth-out-of-it plan is already failing on its own terms: the economy is growing fast with capex booming, yet the deficit is not shrinking and another ~$75 billion in munitions spending is being requested.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Kills the bull case that nominal growth mechanically shrinks the deficit and pulls the long end down.
insights.quote: we're growing pretty fast. Uh we've got capex booming and it doesn't appear like the deficit is shrinking at all. Uh quite the contrary.

insights.claim: In the next recession the Fed's balance sheet could plausibly reach well over $15 trillion and possibly $20 trillion, because the deficit spending required will have to be funded by the printing press.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: The magnitude anchor for a debasement trade — sizes the gold and hard-asset thesis against a specific balance-sheet path.
insights.quote: you could easily see the Fed's balance sheet, you know, at well over 15 trillion. Does it get to 20 trillion?

insights.claim: The current federal deficit is around $2 trillion and could reach roughly $6 trillion in the next recession, per Michael Pento, with Pomboy agreeing on the direction and magnitude.
insights.speaker: host (Adam), citing Michael Pento; endorsed by Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: A recession is not a duration rally in this framework — it triples the supply the long end must absorb.
insights.quote: he's focused on the current two trillion deficit that we have right now and he says when we go into recession next that's going to be like a six trillion deficit

themes.theme: Pension Underfunding and the Coming Bailout

insights.claim: US public and private pensions are underfunded by roughly $4 trillion, improved from about $6 trillion a few years ago — but that improved figure exists only because markets are at or near all-time highs.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Pension solvency is a levered call on the equity market; an ordinary bear market re-opens a multi-trillion hole and forces policy response.
insights.quote: we've now you know managed to whittle it down to just $4 trillion in underfunding um at a time when as we've talked about the markets are hitting all-time record highs

insights.claim: Pension funds' large exposure to alternative assets — private equity and private credit — is a hidden second layer of risk, with some of those positions already being marked at 50 cents on the dollar or less.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Reported pension funded ratios are overstated by stale alternatives marks; secondary-market pricing is the tell.
insights.quote: obviously we're seeing marks in some of those that are 50 cents on the dollar or even less

insights.claim: A pension bailout is the likely policy outcome — Pomboy expects policymakers will not let pensions take the hit even though many are already technically bankrupt, and expects it under a business-as-usual administration, not only a left-leaning one.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Another multi-trillion claim on the printing press that is not in consensus deficit forecasts — bullish hard assets, bearish long-end duration.
insights.quote: to me, this is where the bailout comes because we bailed out the banks in 2008 to an enormous public outcry saying this was just, you know, egregious

insights.claim: Pomboy attributes the original $6 trillion pension funding hole to the Fed's zero-interest-rate policy, arguing bad policy created the problem and more bad policy will be the solution.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Frames the policy loop: rate suppression forces pensions into alternatives, which then requires bailouts financed by money creation.
insights.quote: part of the problem originally, and what drove them into that 6 trillion dollar funding hole, uh years ago was this 0% Fed funds rate policy, the ZER policy that basically, you know, rendered a lot of these uh, pension funds effectively bankrupt

insights.claim: A pension bailout would trigger sharper social blowback than the 2008 bank bailouts or student-loan forgiveness because the resentment is peer-to-peer — a private-sector worker watching a neighbor with a government pension made whole at his expense.
insights.speaker: host (Adam)
insights.so_what: Political constraint on the bailout path could delay or distort it, raising volatility around the eventual policy response.

themes.theme: Deglobalization as a Secular Rate Regime Change

insights.claim: Just as the fall of the Berlin Wall and the onset of globalization pushed rates steadily lower from 1980 until a few years ago, deglobalization should beget the reverse — rates creeping higher year after year over decades.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Argues the 40-year bond bull was a globalization artifact, so mean-reversion trades in duration are fighting a secular regime, not a cycle.
insights.quote: just as you know the fall of the Berlin wall and the onset of globalization thereafter pushed rates steadily lower from 1980 till basically just a few years ago. So will delization I think beget the reverse

insights.claim: A multipolar, deglobalized world is structurally less reliant on the dollar and by extension on US Treasuries, which is already visible in China and Japan reducing or selling Treasury holdings.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy and host
insights.so_what: Shrinking foreign official demand is a persistent term-premium tailwind independent of the US fiscal path.

insights.claim: Reshoring for national-security reasons is inherently inflationary because domestic labor costs more than the offshore labor it replaces, which feeds back into higher rates over time.
insights.speaker: host (Adam), affirmed by Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Policy-driven inflation floor means real yields must stay elevated; favors input suppliers over margin-sensitive importers.

insights.claim: Pomboy's 'bathtub' model: when inflation and rates rise, the real economy consumes a larger share of each marginal dollar of liquidity, siphoning off the flow that previously spilled into financial assets and drove decades of stock and bond bull markets.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for why multiple expansion structurally reverses in an inflationary regime — the core justification for rotating out of paper assets.
insights.quote: If we get into a period where inflation and interest rates steadily move higher the economy is going to suck more and more of that marginal liquidity in to run which is going to siphon therefore money that otherwise would have flowed to financial assets.

insights.claim: The era of throwing a dart at a dartboard and making money in stocks is over; the next regime requires actual fundamental analysis and DCF work to identify which companies perform when the cost of capital, goods and labor is structurally higher.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Implies a regime shift from passive/index beta toward stock selection and dispersion strategies.
insights.quote: the days of easy money are easy wins where you could just throw a dart at a a dart board and make money in a stock are probably behind us

insights.claim: Hard assets that cannot be manufactured out of thin air become more appealing precisely because paper issuance — stocks and bonds from both the private sector and government — is running at unprecedented scale.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: The relative-supply argument is the cleanest formulation of the commodities-over-financial-assets trade.
insights.quote: having hard assets that just can't be manufactured out of thin air strikes me as uh you know an investment with a a very uh appealing attribute to it

insights.claim: The commodity complex versus the S&P 500 is still bouncing around secular lows, and Pomboy expects that ratio to reverse and commodities to outperform financial assets on a relative basis.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy, prompted by host citing Tavi Costa's charts
insights.so_what: A specific, chartable relative-value trade: long commodity complex versus short broad equity index.

insights.claim: Investors can participate in the AI capex boom while staying in hard assets by owning energy and the input sectors the buildout depends on, including copper — an AI bull logically has to be an energy and copper bull.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy and host
insights.so_what: A way to express AI upside without paying AI multiples or carrying depreciation and mark-to-market risk.
insights.quote: you can still be positioning this capex boom and be in a protected hard assets by having exposure to energy and that entire sector um upon which that AI capex depends

insights.claim: Cyclical forces — a next-recession deficit near $6 trillion plus a forced Fed balance-sheet expansion — will add turbo juice to the secular hard-asset trend, since more printed dollars chase the same finite quantity of hard assets.
insights.speaker: host (Adam), affirmed by Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Recession is a buy signal for hard assets in this framework, not a sell signal — the opposite of classic cyclical positioning.

insights.claim: July delivered the worst month for the NASDAQ in 25 years, the biggest July bond-yield spike since 2005, and the largest July oil price spike in over 30 years, yet the S&P was back near record highs within days.
insights.speaker: host (Adam)
insights.so_what: The divergence between realized macro shocks and index levels is the complacency setup Pomboy is trading against.
insights.quote: it was the worst July for the NASDAQ in 25 years. It was the worst uh or the the highest bond spike in July since 2005

insights.claim: Oil has pulled back to about $76 on Iran deal headlines but keeps oscillating between roughly $75 and $85 with no signed agreement, and the long-term direction of travel for oil and commodities is higher.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Treat headline-driven dips toward $75 as accumulation zones if you share the secular commodity view; the risk premium is not priced out.
insights.quote: the direction of travel for oil and commodity prices more broadly long-term is higher

insights.claim: Equity markets are glomming onto profit numbers that are not what they appear while brushing off powerful headwinds from higher rates and higher oil prices — the risks are being priced in credit but not equities.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Summarizes the asymmetry: equity investors are paid nothing for risks credit is already charging for.
insights.quote: the markets are sort of uh being rather insush so shall we say about a lot of these risks out there and are glomming onto profit numbers that that aren't all that they appear on the surface

insights.claim: Pomboy has made no major portfolio changes since the prior month: she is waiting for gold to recover its footing, has increased exposure to the energy sector, holds a little dry powder in T-bills, and is making no material bets in the Treasury market.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Her stated book is the cleanest read on conviction: energy added, gold held, duration deliberately avoided until yields show more damage.
insights.quote: I'm just hanging on waiting for gold to uh recover its footing um and still you know I had increase some of my exposure to the energy sector

insights.claim: Pomboy expects there will eventually be an opportunity to buy Treasuries but says you have to wait to see more damage first, implying she believes long yields have further to rise before the trade turns.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: An explicit 'not yet' on the long-bond capitulation trade from a structural bond bear — a timing marker to revisit.
insights.quote: I think there will come a point when there'll be an opportunity to buy there, but I think you've got to wait to see a little bit more

insights.claim: Pomboy's endgame view is a cathartic cleansing of bubble excesses accumulated since 2000 — not just since COVID — built up through serial monetary bailouts and the Fed put, after which reasonable valuations would set the table for a phenomenal next several decades.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Long-horizon framing: she is positioning for the reset, not the next quarter, and explicitly says this plays out over years to a decade-plus.
insights.quote: basically I'm looking for that catharsis where we do finally cleanse all of these bubble excesses that frankly have been built up since 2000

insights.claim: Consensus positioning has flipped from expecting Fed rate cuts this year to expecting hikes, while the long end of the yield curve is 'going bananas' and the Bank of Japan is out of control defending its currency.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Pomboy
insights.so_what: Documents a violent repricing of rate expectations within a single year — the destabilizing backdrop for any duration-sensitive asset.
insights.quote: they were supposed to come into the year and cut rates. Now everyone thinks they're going to raise rates along into the yield curve is going bananas
